text: Most analyses start with a file. A finance team exports a CSV, an analyst emails an Excel workbook, an application hands you JSON. pandas can read and write all three with a matching pair of functions — read underscore something to load, to underscore something to save. This lesson covers the options that matter in practice, especially for messy real-world files.

Here's a small practice orders table — an order id, a customer name, an amount with one missing value, and a date written as plain text. We'll save and reload this same data in each of the three formats this lesson covers.

Save it with to underscore csv, passing index equals False, then read it straight back with read underscore csv. Check dtypes afterward, and order underscore date comes back as object — plain text — because CSV simply has no date type of its own; you have to ask for real dates explicitly. Without index equals False on the way out, pandas writes the row numbers as an extra unnamed column, and the next read_csv loads it right back as Unnamed colon 0.

Read underscore csv has a lot of arguments, but a handful you'll use constantly. Usecols keeps only the columns you actually need. Dtype sets types up front, like forcing order underscore id to a string. Parse underscore dates converts text straight into real datetimes on the way in. And nrows lets you peek at just the first few rows of a huge file before committing to loading the whole thing.

Files don't always follow the same conventions. A European-style file might use a semicolon as the delimiter and a comma as the decimal point, with N slash A or a bare dash standing in for missing values. Pass sep equals semicolon to set the delimiter, decimal equals comma so 1 comma 5 reads as 1.5, and na underscore values with a list of extra strings that should count as missing — N slash A and dash both become NaN, and the amount column comes out as a proper float64 instead of text.

Excel needs a one-time pip install of openpyxl — without it, these calls fail with a ModuleNotFoundError. To underscore excel writes a workbook with a named sheet; read underscore excel reads it back the same way. To write several sheets into one workbook, use ExcelWriter as a context manager — write the orders to an Orders sheet and a describe summary to a Summary sheet in the same file. Read it back with sheet underscore name equals None, and you get a dictionary of DataFrames, one per sheet.

To underscore json with orient equals records gives you a list of objects, one per row — the exact shape most web APIs use. A missing amount gets written out as null. Read underscore json loads it straight back, but remember dates come back as plain text in JSON too, so convert them with pd dot to underscore datetime after loading, just like with CSV.

Real JSON often has objects nested inside objects, and lists nested inside records — json underscore normalize flattens that. Take a nested structure where each record has a customer object and a list of line items. Pass record underscore path equals items to expand that list into its own rows, and meta with id and the nested customer dot name to copy those parent fields onto every expanded row. The result is a clean flat table — one row per item, with the parent's id and customer name carried along.

To recap: to underscore csv with index equals False, and read underscore csv, handle CSV — sep, decimal, na_values, usecols, dtype, parse_dates, and nrows tame messy files. Excel needs openpyxl, with sheet_name and ExcelWriter for multiple sheets. For JSON, orient equals records gives lists of rows, and json underscore normalize flattens nested structures. Always check dtypes right after loading, whatever the format. Next: querying SQL databases from Python.
